Agen
ah-ZHAHN
n. (the Garonne town of the Huguenot potter Bernard Palissy, who was imprisoned for the gospel and died in the Bastille)
French Agen, from Latin Aginnum, of Gallic origin; the town stands on the Garonne between Bordeaux and Toulouse.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Agen is the Garonne town where a working potter became one of the Reformation's most unusual confessors. Bernard Palissy, born near Agen about 1510, was a glass-painter and surveyor who spent sixteen years in poverty teaching himself to make enamelled earthenware, burning his own furniture to fire his kilns, and succeeded: his rustic ware, moulded with fish, lizards and shells cast from life, made him famous and eventually got him a royal appointment and lodgings in the Tuileries. He was also a self-taught natural philosopher who lectured in Paris on springs, fossils and agriculture, and argued from the fossil shells of the Ardennes that they were the remains of real creatures, which the schools of his day denied. And he was a Reformed Protestant from the 1540s. He was imprisoned at Bordeaux in 1562 and saved only by the intervention of the constable Montmorency, who wanted his pottery; he was arrested again as an old man after the League took Paris, refused to recant, was condemned, and died in the Bastille about 1590 in his eightieth year. The dictionary enters Agen because Palissy is what the Reformation looked like in a workshop, and because he was offered his liberty for a word and did not say it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a potter as one who makes earthen vessels; enamel as a substance of the nature of glass; a kiln as a furnace for baking; and a fossil as a substance dug out of the earth.

expand to see more

POTTER, n. One whose occupation is to make earthen vessels; one who makes pots.

ENAMEL, n. A substance of the nature of glass, differing from it by a greater degree of fusibility or opacity.

KILN, n. A fabric of brick or stone, which may be heated for the purpose of hardening, burning or drying.

FOSSIL, n. A substance dug out of the earth; in modern usage, the petrified remains of animals or plants.

RECANT, v. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to unsay what has been said.

Key Scripture

Jer 18:6 — "O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel."

Isa 64:8 — "But now, O LORD, thou art our father; we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand."

2Co 4:7 — "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us."

Mat 10:32 — "Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven."

Modern Corruption

Garonne town where the Huguenot potter Bernard Palissy was born about 1510, who refused to recant and died in the Bastille about 1590.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the recantation bought with a man's craft. Palissy was useful: a constable saved him from a Bordeaux prison in 1562 because the king's works wanted his enamels, and at the end he was offered his life for a word and refused it at nearly eighty. The dictionary records that he was spared once for his usefulness and killed at last for his confession, and that the second is the measure of the man. “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32) is what he acted on in the Bastille.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the figure a potter's whole life was lived inside. “Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand” (Jer 18:6) is said to a nation, and the prophet's confession is the creature's proper answer: “we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand” (Isa 64:8). Palissy made vessels for kings and was himself one of the vessels the apostle describes, for “we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God” (2Co 4:7).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yotser (H3335), a potter, a former; Hebrew chomer (H2563), clay; Greek ostrakinos (G3749), of earthenware.

expand to see more

Hebrew yotser (H3335) — a potter, one who forms or fashions; “as the clay is in the potter's hand”, Jeremiah 18:6.

Hebrew chomer (H2563) — clay, mire, mortar; “we are the clay, and thou our potter”, Isaiah 64:8.

Hebrew maaseh (H4639) — a work, a deed, a thing made; “we all are the work of thy hand”, Isaiah 64:8.

Greek ostrakinos (G3749) — made of earthenware, of baked clay; “we have this treasure in earthen vessels”, 2 Corinthians 4:7.

Greek homologeo (G3670) — to confess, to say the same thing; “shall confess me before men”, Matthew 10:32.

Usage

"“as the clay is in the potter's hand” (Jer 18:6) — sixteen years of poverty learning to fire enamel."

"“we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2Co 4:7) — a potter spared in 1562 because his work was wanted."

"“shall confess me before men” (Mat 10:32) — condemned at nearly eighty and dead in the Bastille about 1590."
